author: ohtadmin
title: Mello lauds town's blizzard response
text:
The financial impact of the blizzard that dropped 29 inches of snow during the Feb. 22-23 storm has yet to be determined.
“We’re still working at calculating that,” Town Administrator Ed Mello said. “We’re not looking at a knee-jerk reaction.” Mello, who said it costs about $900 hourly when the staff is working overtime, briefed the town councilors Monday at their meeting.
He said it was a combination of tree trimming, cooperation from residents, investment in equipment, communication between departments, such as plow trucks helping ambulances, and the “commitment of the staff that really put us in a better place than most communities.”
“It’s like a game of dominos,” he said. “We were very fortunate that we didn’t have a lot of dominoes fall. At the end of the day, I really need to commend all of the staff.”
Mello, who “enjoyed” plowing during the blizzard opposed to being indoors — “there’s something about the power of Mother Nature” — said he refused aid from Connecticut, Vermont, Maine and New Hampshire.
“We were offered that opportunity and did request those resources early on, but by the time those resources became available Thursday into Friday, our staff was in such a great place in terms of clearing the roads, I really didn’t see that it would be useful to bring those resources in,” he said. “Candidly, while other communities still hadn’t touched a road, I felt it more appropriate to allocate those resources to them.”
Mello said the department of public works was working with 100% of its equipment until Tuesday, when the fleet’s oldest truck, which is slated for replacement, was disabled. Aside from that truck, the “occasional flat tire” and a sander that went out of service, “by and large, the investment in our equipment really paid off to provide the best response that we could.”
Mello, however, did hire contractors with backhoes and front-end loaders to help clear the 5-foot-high snow drifts. Even the largest town plows could not get through those piles.
Mello also credited his staff’s strategy. While the director of public works, Mike Gray, did pull some of the plows off the roads during the height of the storm because it was “self-defeating” with trucks getting stuck, getting them back into service sooner rather than later “put us in our best position.”
“A lot of communities didn’t do that,” Mello said. “By the time they put trucks back on the roads, they had 30 inches of snow.”
There is the potential for reimbursement from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, according to Mello, of 75%. First, however, the state of Rhode Island must “submit a preliminary determination related to damages.”
“That’s yet to be determined,” he said. “There’s a long way to go before that happens.”
Mello credited the “tremendous effort” to get the schools open by Friday after they were “literally buried in snow.”
He also lauded the volunteers at the fire department, some of whom left their houses Sunday and didn’t return until Tuesday, for responding to 19 calls during the blizzard.
“That’s a significant amount of calls,” he said, “and every call is a challenge.”
